Legumes such as beans, lentils, chickpeas and soy, along with grains, nuts and seeds, provide all the protein and all the essential amino acids an adult needs, as long as the diet is varied and supplies enough energy. Nutrition bodies in several countries, such as the US Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics and Brazil's Federal Council of Nutritionists, recognize that well-planned vegan diets can be adequate at all stages of life; others, such as the German Nutrition Society, don't yet take a position for pregnant women, children and older people, and call for professional supervision.
"Where do you get your protein? Without meat you'll be weak. You need quality protein."
Human beings need protein, with all the essential amino acids.
Animal foods are concentrated, complete sources of protein.
It's hard to get enough complete protein from plants alone.
So we need to eat animal products.
P1 and P2 are true. The problem lies in P3: the evidence shows that varied plant diets provide enough complete protein for adults.

Protein helps the body grow and get strong. And it isn't only in meat! Beans, lentils, chickpeas, peanuts and soy have lots of protein. Rice and beans, for example, is a great combination. And lots of people, even athletes, don't eat meat and get all the protein they need.

We need protein, not animal protein. Beans, lentils, chickpeas, soy, tofu, nuts and grains provide all the protein and all the amino acids we need, as long as we eat a varied diet over the day and in sufficient quantity. There's no need to combine foods in the same meal. The US Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics and Brazil's Federal Council of Nutritionists recognize that well-planned vegan diets can be adequate at all stages of life. Rice and beans, a staple from Brazil to Mexico to the Caribbean, is already an excellent source of protein.
"If beans, lentils and soy provide all the protein we need, is the need for protein or for meat?"
The argument confuses the nutrient with the source:
Meat, eggs, milk, but also beans, lentils, chickpeas, soy, tofu, nuts, grains
Plant foods contain all nine essential amino acids, but in different proportions: cereals are low in lysine, which legumes make up for. Variety over the day solves it
A 2019 review concluded that protein-rich foods such as legumes, nuts and seeds are enough to ensure protein adequacy for adults on vegetarian and vegan diets.

text.bold: 2. The amino acids are in plants.

paragraph.text: The idea that foods must be combined in the same meal is an old myth. Eating a varied diet over the day provides all the essential amino acids (G2).

The US Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics states that well-planned vegan diets are healthy, nutritionally adequate and appropriate for all stages of life, including pregnancy, childhood and for athletes. In Brazil, the Federal Council of Nutritionists says the same in a 2022 technical opinion. It isn't unanimous: the German Nutrition Society considers a vegan diet adequate for healthy adults but, for lack of data, neither recommends nor advises against it for pregnant women, children and older people, and calls for professional supervision. None of these bodies says animal protein is necessary.

text.bold: 4. Traditional plates are already rich in protein.

paragraph.text: Rice and beans, dal and rice, hummus and bread: traditional combinations around the world provide good-quality protein.

Chickens and pigs get their protein from soy and corn feed; cattle, from pasture and grain, with the help of rumen microorganisms that the human digestive system lacks. So it doesn't work to say "if the ox gets strong eating grass, so would we": the digestion is different. The point is another: eating the animal means getting, by a longer route and with more losses, nutrients that came from plants, and humans get enough protein by eating legumes, grains and seeds directly.
Legumes, nuts and seeds are enough for protein adequacy in adults on vegetarian and vegan diets
Well-planned vegan diets are appropriate at all stages of life

The most serious version grants that healthy adults get enough protein from plants, but points out that older people, children and athletes have greater needs, and that some vegans eat less protein than they should, especially those who eat little overall. Mariotti and Gardner's review acknowledges these risks and adds that the digestibility of plant protein is only a few percentage points lower.

This is an indirect argument: it doesn't say animals don't matter, but that we need them. Since the need doesn't hold for those with access to a varied diet, the question returns to its starting point: if we don't need it, what justifies making animals suffer and die?

paragraph.text: The principle being tested is: "if a food contains a nutrient, we need that food".
We'd need oranges, not any fruit with vitamin C
We'd need milk, not other sources
This is the argument of G5

Concern about nutrition is legitimate. Protein is essential, and any diet, vegan or not, needs to be planned to provide enough. Some groups, such as older people and children, deserve special attention.
But the need is for protein, not for animals. With beans, lentils, soy and variety, protein is covered, and the moral question becomes the main one again: if we don't need it, why carry on?
